questions.question: Forced to choose between large-workspace performance and enterprise summaries, a PM says: "Performance first, then summaries." Why is this not yet a decision?
options: Because the engineering estimate for performance work has not been produced
Because summaries have a larger revenue base and should therefore go first
Because sequencing decisions require sign-off from the account manager
Because it names an order without naming what the delay to summaries costs, or who bears it
questions.explanation: Sequencing displaces the second option by the duration of the first, and that delay has a cost and a payer. Option A is the tempting one: an estimate would sharpen the sequence, but you could have a perfect estimate and still have recorded no trade-off.

questions.question: A PM justifies the performance work: "Slow workspaces put paid seats at risk, so this is clearly worth doing." What is the reasoning error?
options: The 34% figure came from monitoring rather than from customers
The work is being compared to doing nothing, not to the best alternative use of the same engineers
P95 response time is not a user-facing metric
4% of workspaces is too small a population to justify a cycle of work
questions.explanation: An option can be positive against inaction and still be a loss against what those same engineers would otherwise have built. Option D is the answer a PM gives after learning to check population size — but a small population holding a disproportionate share of paid seats may well be worth it. The error is the missing comparison, not the size.

questions.question: An engineering lead says the team can shift "about 40% of capacity" from the migration to performance work. What should the PM check first?
options: Whether 40% is enough to complete the performance work this cycle
Whether the remaining 60% still meets the migration deadline
Whether the same specific engineers are the only ones who can do both, making the capacity non-substitutable
Whether 40% has been agreed with the founder before it is committed
questions.explanation: Capacity expressed as a percentage hides whether the resource is a pool of hours or two specific people. If they are the same two, moving 40% may mean moving all of the only people who can do either. Options A and B both reason correctly inside a false premise — they treat the percentage as real before checking whether it is.

questions.question: A PM writes a full five-face trade-off record for a decision about which of two empty-state copy variants to ship. Both are reversible within a day. What is the problem?
options: The record costs more than the decision, and the habit slows the team where speed was free
Copy changes should be owned by design, so the record is written by the wrong person
Nothing — consistent documentation is what makes trade-offs comparable over time
The record should have used a single face, reversal cost, rather than all five
questions.explanation: The boundary of the model is consequence multiplied by reversal cost. Option C is the trained answer — consistency sounds like discipline, but a team that documents every trade-off documents them badly and pays the process cost exactly where it earns nothing.

questions.question: After the decision to fund performance work is announced, the PM writes a trade-off record explaining why summaries lost. How should this document be treated?
options: As a decision record, since it contains all five faces of the trade-off
As evidence that the decision was sound, since it survived being written down
As invalid, because trade-off records written after a decision have no use
As a rationale, labelled as such, and kept out of the evidence base as if it were a decision record
questions.explanation: Once a choice is announced, every face of it can be described so that the choice looks correct. The document may still be useful for communicating the decision. Option C over-corrects — the failure is not writing it, it is letting a defence enter the record as if it were analysis.
